title: Job 35:9–16
context: Elihu continues his speech by explaining why the cries of the oppressed may go unanswered: few seek God their Maker, who gives songs in the night, and God does not regard empty cries rooted in pride. He closes by charging that Job multiplies words without knowledge. The line about God who gives songs in the night is warm and hopeful, whatever one’s view of Elihu. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about sincere prayer and humility, while weighing Elihu’s application to Job.

verses.text: “By reason of the multitude of oppressions they cry out. They cry for help by reason of the arm of the mighty.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu says people cry out under many oppressions and call for help against the arm of the mighty. Suffering is widespread.

Arminian readers see the real cries of the oppressed acknowledged.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elihu begins to explain why such cries may go unanswered.

Reformed readers see human misery under the power of the mighty. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the reality of oppression and the cries it produces, which Scripture takes seriously throughout.

verses.text: But no one says, ‘Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night,
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu laments that no one says, ‘Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night?’ The line is beautiful.

Arminian readers warmly see God giving hope and praise in dark times.
verses.reformedNotes:
Whatever one concludes about Elihu, the image of God who gives songs in the night is a warm and hopeful one.

Reformed readers likewise treasure the picture of God sustaining his people in darkness. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground.

verses.text: who teaches us more than the animals of the earth, and makes us wiser than the birds of the sky?’
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu continues: God teaches people more than the animals and makes them wiser than the birds. Human dignity is God’s gift.

Arminian readers see God’s gracious gift of understanding to humanity.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse completes the question of verse 10, describing God as teacher.

Reformed readers see wisdom as God’s gift. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the dignity God gives human beings and their capacity to seek him.

verses.text: There they cry, but no one answers, because of the pride of evil men.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu says they cry out but receive no answer, because of the pride of evil men. Pride blocks the cry.

Arminian readers see pride hindering a genuine turning to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elihu’s explanation is general. Whether it applies to Job, whose cries the book presents sympathetically, is part of the wider debate about Elihu.

Reformed readers see pride as a barrier to prayer. Both traditions read this as shared ground about humility in prayer.

verses.text: Surely God will not hear an empty cry, neither will the Almighty regard it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu says God will not hear an empty cry, nor will the Almighty regard it. Sincerity matters.

Arminian readers affirm that God seeks sincere hearts in prayer rather than mere words.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elihu implies that some cries are empty, though he does not prove that Job’s are.

Reformed readers see the necessity of true prayer. Both traditions read this as shared ground about sincere prayer, while weighing Elihu’s implication about Job carefully.

verses.text: How much less when you say you don’t see him. The cause is before him, and you wait for him!
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu says how much less will God hear when Job says he does not see him, though the case is before God and Job waits. He addresses Job’s complaint.

Arminian readers see an appeal to patient waiting.
verses.reformedNotes:
Job had lamented that he could not find God (23:8–9). The verse’s exact sense is debated.

Reformed readers see a call to trust while waiting. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: But now, because he has not visited in his anger, neither does he greatly regard arrogance,
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu says that because God has not visited in anger, nor greatly regarded arrogance, the next verse follows. He argues from God’s restraint.

Arminian readers see God’s patience mentioned, though Elihu uses it to criticize Job.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse is difficult, and translations vary. Elihu seems to suggest that Job has taken God’s restraint lightly.

Reformed readers see God’s forbearance. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hold the sense tentatively.

verses.text: therefore Job opens his mouth with empty talk, and he multiplies words without knowledge.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu concludes that Job opens his mouth with empty talk and multiplies words without knowledge. The speech ends in rebuke.

Arminian readers report this as Elihu’s verdict, to be weighed with the rest of the book.
verses.reformedNotes:
The LORD will later speak of words “without knowledge” (38:2), yet also commend Job over the three friends (42:7). Readers differ on how Elihu fits.

Reformed readers weigh his charge. Both traditions read this as shared ground.
